title: the words, line by line, from Luke
hook: the words, line by line, from Luke
tomorrow: the most misunderstood room in the building

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rosary beads: five decades, a counting string. Your line was: hands busy, heart free. Today, the words on those ten beads. Day eleven.

At a wake, a room full of voices runs it together until it sounds like one long word. A kid in Catholic school rattles it off before anyone can blink. In football, a quarterback throws the ball deep with no hope left, and that pass still gets called a Hail Mary. Said that fast, it's easy to miss where the words came from, and who said them first. Half the prayer isn't new at all. It's lifted, line by line, from the first chapter of Luke's Gospel. Today, slowly.
screen: `ONE LONG WORD AT A WAKE.` → `A HAIL MARY PASS.` → `LIFTED FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: The first line belongs to an angel. Remember day six, Gabriel in the room in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, his first words are: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail is just an old hello. Full of grace is your first word, on day one: a gift given, filled to the brim. The next line belongs to a relative. A little later in Luke, Mary goes to visit her cousin Elizabeth, who's also pregnant, and Elizabeth cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over the centuries Christians put those two greetings side by side, an angel's and a cousin's, and added two names: Mary, right after the angel's hail, and Jesus at the end. That's the whole first half. Every word of it, apart from those two names, is from Luke. Then the prayer turns. The second half isn't scripture. It's the Church speaking, and it came into the prayer later. It goes: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Listen to the shape. The first half says hello. The second half asks for something. And what it asks is small and huge at once: pray for us. Now, and at the very end. Catholics aren't asking Mary to do what only God does. They're asking her to pray with them, the way you'd ask anyone you trust to pray for you. On the rosary it's said ten times in each decade. A greeting, then a request, again and again, like a heartbeat, while the mind thinks about Jesus. Say it fast and it's a blur. Say it slowly and you're standing in two rooms in Luke's Gospel.
screen: `AN ANGEL'S HELLO.` · `A COUSIN'S BLESSING.` · `THEN THE CHURCH ASKS.` · `PRAY FOR US, NOW AND AT THE END.` · then, large: `A GREETING, THEN A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Let your breath slow down. On the breath in, think of a greeting: hello to someone you love. On the breath out, think of a request: one thing you need right now. In, a greeting. Out, a request. If you pray the Hail Mary, you can say it once, as slowly as you've ever said it. The bell holds the time.
The rosary, the Hail Mary. An angel's hello and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then the Church's request: pray for us. Eleventh word.
screen: `THE ROSARY, THE HAIL MARY — your 11th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a greeting, then a request. Today, before you ask anyone for anything, greet them first, properly. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD ROOM IN THE BUILDING.`

howItsDone: Catholics say the Hail Mary ten times on each decade of the rosary, and on its own at many moments of the day; its first half comes from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.

fork.setup: Mary, newly pregnant, walks into her cousin Elizabeth's house. what does Elizabeth say?

original.note: Latin: hail Mary, full of grace. the opening of the prayer in the Church's old language.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fast prayer, or a desperate football pass.
what it means: an angel's greeting and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then a request: pray for us.
what a scholar hears: Luke 1:28 and 1:42 joined in medieval devotion; the petition added later and fixed in the Roman Breviary of Pius V; kecharitomene, the Greek behind full of grace.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook drops the unsourced superlative 'the prayer people say fastest', 'eight seconds' and two 'most people' claims; teach cuts the 'sixteenth century' date and the false causal 'that's why it's said ten times'; 'ask a mother' changed so it doesn't repeat day 6; trapdoor drops the year 1568 (Pius V's Breviary kept, for a Keeper to confirm).
Luke 1:28 and 1:42 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
The second half's standard form: generally dated to the 1568 Roman Breviary of Pius V; the voice says 'settled in the sixteenth century'. Confirm.
The traditional English Hail Mary is quoted in the voice without quotation marks; confirm it is fine to present it as a traditional public-domain text.
Hail Mary pass: popularized by Roger Staubach in 1975; confirm.

Voice now says two names were added to Luke's words (Mary and Jesus); the earlier draft said one name, then referred to 'those two names'. Pairing the two greetings is older in Eastern liturgies, so the scholar line now says 'joined in Western devotion by the Middle Ages'. Confirm dating.
